module.title: Unit 5: What a Story!: Past Perfect & Narrative Tenses
module.objective: Mampu menceritakan kisah menggunakan relative pronouns, relative clauses (defining dan non-defining), dan memahami berbagai jenis cerita serta elemen-elemennya

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Storytellers and Plot Twists
subModules.vocabularyFocus: Storytelling, Film Blockbusters, and Literary Devices

content.summary: Welcome to the reading mission for Unit 5. In this module, you will explore how writers use the past perfect and narrative tenses to sequence events in stories. You will read engaging texts about traditional storytellers and modern Hollywood blockbusters, examining how narrative timing creates suspense and interest.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Past Simple for main actions, Past Continuous for background descriptions, and Past Perfect for actions completed before another past action.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Terms related to storytelling, narrative plots, film production, and literary characters.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning for chronological sequence markers and identifying relationships between background events and main plot points.

learningObjectives: Comprehend the main ideas and details of texts about storytelling traditions and modern cinema.
Distinguish between background actions and completed past events using narrative tenses.
Identify key vocabulary words related to plots, villains, and literary openings.

contextWarmup.prompt: When you read a mystery novel or watch a thriller film, why is it important for the writer to establish the background before introducing the main conflict?
options: It helps the audience understand what characters were doing before the main event happened.
It ensures that the story has no dialogues or character descriptions.
It makes the book shorter and easier to finish in one evening.
contextWarmup.explanation: Establishing background using narrative tenses allows readers to grasp the scene and context before the main plot twists occur.

rules: Use the Past Simple for completed sequential actions in a story.
Use the Past Continuous for longer background actions interrupted by short actions.
Use the Past Perfect (had plus past participle) for actions that happened before another past action.

commonTrap.trapTitle: Confusing Past Simple and Past Perfect
commonTrap.explanation: Learners often use the Past Simple for all past events, even when one clearly happened before another.
commonTrap.wrong: When I arrived at the cinema, the film started.
commonTrap.correct: When I arrived at the cinema, the film had already started.

paragraphs: Long before books were printed or films were produced, communities relied on oral traditions. A traditional storyteller was a vital member of society, travelling from village to village to share tales that had been handed down through centuries. When the storyteller arrived in a settlement, villagers eagerly offered food and shelter in exchange for entertainment and news from distant places.

Today, storytelling has transformed into modern media such as Hollywood blockbusters and bestselling novels. Although the technology has changed, the core elements remain identical. A fascinating plot, a complex villain, and an engaging opening are still essential for capturing the audience. Writers carefully construct suspense so that readers remain hooked until the final climax.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Crafting Compelling Narrative Stories with Relative Clauses

content.summary: Master the art of weaving complex narrative structures using relative clauses, defining versus non-defining modifiers, and precise punctuation to make your stories engaging at a B2 level.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Defining Relative Clauses for Essential Plot Detail
blueprintItems.formula: Main Clause + Relative Pronoun (who/which/that/where/whose) + Defining Detail
blueprintItems.example: The detective who solved the mystery found the hidden diary.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Non-Defining Relative Clauses for Added Background
blueprintItems.formula: Main Clause + Comma + Relative Pronoun (who/which/whose) + Extra Information + Comma
blueprintItems.example: Arthur Conan Doyle, who wrote Sherlock Holmes, studied medicine.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Clause-Modifying 'Which' for Whole Actions
blueprintItems.formula: Action Clause + , + which + Result or Reaction
blueprintItems.example: The suspect dropped his wallet, which proved his guilt immediately.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always use commas around non-defining relative clauses.
mechanicsRules.badExample: My favorite author who lives in London released a new book yesterday.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: My favorite author, who lives in London, released a new book yesterday.
mechanicsRules.why: Non-defining clauses provide extra information that can be removed without changing the core meaning of the sentence, so they require commas.

mechanicsRules.rule: Do not use commas with defining relative clauses.
mechanicsRules.badExample: The manuscript, that was lost for a century, was finally discovered.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: The manuscript that was lost for a century was finally discovered.
mechanicsRules.why: Defining clauses identify which specific noun you mean, so setting them off with commas is grammatically incorrect.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'whose' to show possession for both people and things.
mechanicsRules.badExample: I met a writer who latest novel became a bestseller.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I met a writer whose latest novel became a bestseller.
mechanicsRules.why: The relative pronoun 'whose' is required to indicate ownership before a noun in relative clauses.

guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three to four sentences introducing a fictional character in a story. Use at least one defining relative clause and one non-defining relative clause.
guidedLabChallenges.example: I met a mysterious woman who wore a heavy velvet coat. She carried an old leather suitcase, which looked extremely heavy. The stranger, whose eyes were remarkably sharp, avoided looking at anyone.
guidedLabChallenges.placeholder: Start typing your narrative sentences here...

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the two sentences using a defining relative clause with 'who':
practicumQuestions.promptText: The journalist uncovered the conspiracy. She won an international award.
practicumQuestions.hint: Replace 'She' with 'who' to connect the sentences.
targetAnswers: The journalist who uncovered the conspiracy won an international award.
The journalist, who uncovered the conspiracy, won an international award.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A defining relative clause uses 'who' immediately after the person noun without separating commas.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the two sentences using a non-defining relative clause with 'which':
practicumQuestions.promptText: The old mansion was built in 1900. It now serves as a local history museum.
practicumQuestions.hint: Add commas around the non-defining clause starting with 'which'.
targetAnswers: The old mansion, which was built in 1900, now serves as a local history museum.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses give extra information about a specific noun and must be enclosed in commas.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Choose the correct relative pronoun to complete the sentence: 'The writer _____ latest novel won the prize gave a speech.'
practicumQuestions.hint: Use the pronoun that indicates possession.
practicumQuestions.explanation: We use 'whose' to indicate possession or ownership preceding a noun ('latest novel').

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct all punctuation, capitalization, and grammar errors in this sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: the detective found a clue that changed the whole case
practicumQuestions.hint: Check the starting capital letter and terminal punctuation.
targetAnswers: The detective found a clue that changed the whole case.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Sentences in English must begin with a capital letter and end with a full stop.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the sentences using 'where':
practicumQuestions.promptText: We visited the coastal village. The mystery of the missing ship began there.
practicumQuestions.hint: Replace 'there' with 'where' to link the location clause.
targetAnswers: We visited the coastal village where the mystery of the missing ship began.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The relative pronoun 'where' is used to refer to a place or location in relative clauses.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a sentence describing a tool or gadget using the relative pronoun 'that' or 'which':
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'A smartphone is a device that...' or 'which...'
targetAnswers: A smartphone is a device that connects people around the world.
A smartphone is a gadget which allows users to browse the internet.
A smartphone is a tool that helps people communicate easily.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Defining relative clauses with 'that' or 'which' effectively describe objects and appliances.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the sentences so that 'which' modifies the entire preceding clause:
practicumQuestions.promptText: The suspect confessed to the crime. This surprised everyone in the courtroom.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use a comma before 'which' to refer to the whole action of confessing.
targetAnswers: The suspect confessed to the crime, which surprised everyone in the courtroom.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Using 'which' after a comma can refer to the entire situation or action described in the main clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fix the punctuation error in this sentence containing a non-defining clause:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Arthur Conan Doyle who created Sherlock Holmes was born in Scotland.
practicumQuestions.hint: Non-defining clauses require commas before and after.
targetAnswers: Arthur Conan Doyle, who created Sherlock Holmes, was born in Scotland.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Since 'who created Sherlock Holmes' is extra information about Arthur Conan Doyle, it must be set off with commas.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'who' instead of 'that' for a person:
practicumQuestions.promptText: She is the author that wrote the bestselling thriller.
practicumQuestions.hint: Replace 'that' with 'who' when referring to a person.
targetAnswers: She is the author who wrote the bestselling thriller.
practicumQuestions.explanation: While 'that' is sometimes used, 'who' is the standard and preferred relative pronoun for people in B2 formal writing.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Create an original sentence about a place you like, using the relative pronoun 'where':
practicumQuestions.hint: Example: I love visiting the cafe where...
targetAnswers: I love visiting the library where I can read in peace.
I remember the small town where I spent my childhood summers.
She went back to the studio where she recorded her first song.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A well-constructed sentence using 'where' properly integrates a location relative clause into a narrative context.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Narrative Tenses & Storytelling Dynamics

content.summary: Mastering narrative speaking requires precise control over narrative tenses, sentence stress, and dramatic intonation. When recounting past events, speakers must balance the past simple for main actions, the past continuous for background scenes, and the past perfect for prior actions.
content.audioGuidance: Focus on pausing briefly before introducing unexpected plot twists. Use rising intonation on dependent clauses to build suspense and falling intonation to resolve narrative points.

pillars.name: Narrative Rhythm
pillars.explanation: Link auxiliary verbs like had with past participles to maintain a natural speaking pace without hesitating.

pillars.name: Dramatic Stress
pillars.target: Emphasizing key vocabulary such as villains, plots, and blockbusters
pillars.explanation: Place primary vocal stress on content words that carry the emotional weight of the story.

pillars.name: Intonation Contours
pillars.target: Using voice pitch to signal flashbacks
pillars.explanation: Lower your vocal pitch slightly when introducing background context using the past perfect tense.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice how compound nouns shift stress depending on their internal syllable structure.
Adjectives often carry stress on the first syllable, similar to common nouns like villain.
Both words maintain primary stress on the initial syllable.
Phrasal verbs stress the main verb root while keeping particles lighter.

drills.targetText: The skilled storyteller had already captivated the audience before the main plot began.

drills.focus: Past perfect auxiliary pronunciation and narrative flow
drills.hint: Pronounce 'had' weakly as /həd/ and link it smoothly to 'already'.

drills.targetText: Villains in Hollywood blockbusters often have fascinating backstories.

drills.focus: Multi-syllable adjective stress and plural endings
drills.hint: Ensure the first syllable of fascinating is sharp and clear.

drills.targetText: Ancient legends were handed down from generation to generation in village shelters.

drills.focus: Connected speech in passive narrative structures
drills.hint: Blend 'handed down' into a single continuous phrase.

drills.targetText: During the exciting opening scene, heavy rain was falling outside.

practicumQuestions.explanation: Use the past perfect tense to explain what happened before the climax.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Use rising intonation for clause transitions and falling intonation for narrative conclusions.
